title: What radiation protection training does the EU Basic Safety Standards Directive require?
description: What Articles 14 and 15 of Directive 2013/59/Euratom require for training exposed workers, plus the roles of radiation protection experts and officers.
shortAnswer: Council Directive 2013/59/Euratom, the EU Basic Safety Standards Directive, requires Member States to ensure radiation protection education, training and information for everyone whose tasks require specific radiation protection competence, repeated at appropriate intervals and documented (Article 14). Article 15 requires undertakings, or the employers of outside workers, to inform exposed workers of radiation risks, procedures and emergency plans and to provide training programs. Member States recognize radiation protection experts and may recognize radiation protection officers.
keyTakeaways: Article 14(1) requires radiation protection training and information to be repeated at appropriate intervals and documented.
Article 15 lists five information topics for exposed workers and requires training programs, with extra content on pregnancy, breastfeeding, and high activity sealed sources.
For outside workers, their own employer must provide training and core information, while the undertaking remains responsible for site specific content.

Radiation protection experts must be recognized by the competent authority and advise on training programs; radiation protection officers supervise practices and train exposed workers where national law requires them.
Member States had to transpose the directive by February 6, 2018, when five earlier Euratom directives were repealed.
jurisdiction: European Union (applied through each Member State's national law)
regulator: National radiation protection competent authorities designated by each Member State; the European Commission monitors transposition under the Euratom Treaty
appliesTo: Undertakings carrying out practices involving ionizing radiation, including industry, research, nuclear, and healthcare
Exposed workers and outside workers who work in controlled or supervised areas
Radiation protection experts, radiation protection officers, and medical physics experts
Emergency workers and staff at installations where orphan sources may be found

sections.heading: What is the EU Basic Safety Standards Directive?

blocks.text: The Basic Safety Standards Directive is [Council Directive 2013/59/Euratom](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32013L0059) of December 5, 2013, which lays down basic safety standards for protection against the dangers arising from exposure to ionizing radiation. It covers occupational, medical, and public exposure in one instrument. Article 106 required Member States to transpose it by February 6, 2018, and Article 107 repealed Directives 89/618/Euratom, 90/641/Euratom, 96/29/Euratom, 97/43/Euratom and 2003/122/Euratom from that date.

It is adopted under the Euratom Treaty rather than as an individual directive under the [OSH Framework Directive](/regulations/eu-osh-framework-directive-training). [EU-OSHA's summary](https://osha.europa.eu/en/legislation/directives/directive-2013-59-euratom-protection-against-ionising-radiation) notes that the directive is addressed to Member States, which must put national implementing laws in place, and that its occupational provisions sit mostly in Chapter VI. As at November 2026, employers comply with their national radiation protection law and the licensing conditions set by their national competent authority.

For context, Article 9 sets the occupational effective dose limit at 20 mSv in any single year, with a limit on equivalent dose to the lens of the eye of 20 mSv in a single year or 100 mSv over five consecutive years, subject to a maximum of 50 mSv in a single year, as specified in national legislation. Training content should reflect the national figures.

sections.heading: What does Article 14 require of the training system?

blocks.text: Article 14 sets the framework that Member States must build. Article 14(1) requires "an adequate legislative and administrative framework ensuring the provision of appropriate radiation protection education, training and information to all individuals whose tasks require specific competences in radiation protection", and adds that "the provision of training and information shall be repeated at appropriate intervals and documented".

Article 14(2) requires arrangements for education, training and retraining so that radiation protection experts and medical physics experts, as well as occupational health services and dosimetry services, can be recognized in relation to the type of practice. Article 14(3) lets Member States set up the same for radiation protection officers, if their national law provides for that recognition. The documentation requirement in Article 14(1) is unusual among EU safety directives and makes training records a direct compliance item.

sections.heading: What must exposed workers be told and trained on under Article 15?

blocks.text: Article 15(1) requires the undertaking to inform exposed workers on five topics, and Article 15(4) requires appropriate radiation protection training and information programs for them. The five information topics are:

items: the radiation health risks involved in their work
the general radiation protection procedures and precautions to be taken
the procedures and precautions connected with the operational and working conditions of the practice in general and each type of workstation or work to which they may be assigned
the relevant parts of the emergency response plans and procedures
the importance of complying with the technical, medical and administrative requirements

blocks.text: Article 15(2) and (3) add two specific information duties: the importance of an early declaration of pregnancy, in view of the risks to the unborn child, and of announcing the intention to breastfeed, in view of the risks to a breastfed infant after intake of radionuclides or bodily contamination. Article 15(5) requires undertakings responsible for high activity sealed sources to include specific requirements for their safe management and control, with "specific information on the possible consequences of the loss of adequate control".
Outside workers split the duty. For them, their own employer must ensure the information in points (a), (b) and (e) is provided and must provide the training programs.

Article 51(3)(c) then requires the undertaking, before an outside worker enters a controlled area, to ensure that in addition to basic radiation protection training the worker has received specific instructions and training on the workplace and the activities, in line with points (c) and (d) of Article 15(1). For supervised areas, Article 51(3)(d) requires working instructions appropriate to the radiological risk. Article 37(1) reinforces this for controlled areas: access is limited to individuals who have received appropriate instructions, and the worker "shall receive specific training in connection with the characteristics of the workplace and the activities".

sections.heading: What do radiation protection experts and officers do in training?

blocks.text: The radiation protection expert advises on training programs, and the radiation protection officer typically delivers or supervises training on site. The directive defines both roles in Article 4 and sets their tasks in Articles 82 and 84.

blocks.text: Article 84(1) also requires the RPO to report directly to the undertaking and to be given the means needed to carry out their tasks, and lets Member States require employers of outside workers to designate an RPO. Because recognition criteria are set nationally and communicated to the Commission under Article 79(2), an RPE recognized in one Member State is not automatically recognized in another.

blocks.text: A [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix) that separates worker categories (for example classified workers, outside workers, and emergency workers) keeps these duties distinct. Setting the "appropriate intervals" Article 14 requires is covered in [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: Are there extra training rules for medical exposure and orphan sources?

blocks.text: Yes. Article 18 requires that practitioners and individuals involved in practical aspects of medical radiological procedures have adequate education, information and theoretical and practical training, that Member States establish curricula and recognize the corresponding qualifications, and that continuing education and training is provided after qualification, including training on new clinical techniques. Healthcare organizations should read this together with the [healthcare and life sciences industry page](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

Article 16 asks Member States to encourage installations where orphan sources are likely to be found, such as large metal scrap yards, to train workers in visual detection of sources, basic facts about ionizing radiation, and the actions to take on detection. Readers comparing jurisdictions can see a licensing based model in [radiation safety license training in Australia](/regulations/radiation-safety-licence-training-australia).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models the Article 15 topics, local rules, and source specific procedures as linked concepts with assessment points, separated by worker category and site. That structure supports the Article 14 duty to repeat and document training, and makes it clear which content belongs to the undertaking and which to an outside worker's employer.

faqs.q: How often must radiation protection training be repeated?
faqs.a: Directive 2013/59/Euratom does not set a number. Article 14(1) requires training and information to be repeated at appropriate intervals and documented. National law or the competent authority's licensing conditions usually fix the interval, often differently by worker category.

faqs.q: Is a radiation protection officer mandatory in every EU country?
faqs.a: No. Article 84(1) leaves it to each Member State to decide in which practices an RPO must be designated, and recognition of RPOs is optional under Articles 14(3) and 79(1). Recognition arrangements for radiation protection experts, by contrast, are mandatory.

faqs.q: Who trains contractors who work in a controlled area?
faqs.a: Both parties. The outside worker's employer must provide radiation protection training and the general information in Article 15(1)(a), (b) and (e). Under Article 51(3)(c), the undertaking must ensure the worker also has specific instructions and training on the workplace and activities before entering a controlled area.

faqs.q: Does the directive cover radon in workplaces?
faqs.a: Yes. Article 9 applies the occupational dose limits to the sum of exposures, including occupational exposure to radon in workplaces requiring notification under Article 54(3). Where radon exposure is managed as occupational exposure, the information and training duties for exposed workers apply under national law.
